title: 06. Distributed Systems & Consistency: Two Phase Commit (2PC)
summary: Two Phase Commit (2PC) is a distributed-transaction protocol in which a coordinator asks all participants to PREPARE (vote yes/no) in phase 1, then broadcasts COMMIT or ABORT in phase 2 based on whether every participant voted…
objectives: Describe the two phases of 2PC and the role of the coordinator.
Why is 2PC called a "blocking" protocol, and what causes the blocking?
What is the role of the durable log in 2PC, both at the coordinator and at the participants?
What happens if a participant crashes after voting YES, and how does it recover?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Two Phase Commit (2PC) is a distributed-transaction protocol in which a **coordinator** asks all participants to **PREPARE** (vote yes/no) in phase 1, then broadcasts **COMMIT** or **ABORT** in phase 2 based on whether every participant voted yes; it provides strong atomicity but is **blocking** — if the coordinator crashes after participants have prepared, they hold their locks indefinitely, waiting for the decision.

Two Phase Commit is the oldest and most studied distributed-transaction protocol, dating back to Gray's 1978 work and formalized in the X/Open XA standard that underpins Java's JTA, PostgreSQL's prepared transactions, and MySQL's XA transactions. The protocol solves a specific problem: how can `N` independent resource managers (databases, message queues) agree to commit or abort a transaction atomically, given that any of them can crash and the network can drop messages? The answer 2PC gives is: introduce a coordinator whose job is to ask everyone, tally the votes, and broadcast the decision. The coordinator itself is a single point of failure, but its decisions are logged durably so that on restart it can resume the protocol. The protocol's strength is its simplicity and strong atomicity guarantee; its weakness is the blocking behavior when the coordinator fails, which makes it unsuitable for high-availability microservices.

Phase 1 is the **Prepare** (or **Voting**) phase. The coordinator sends a `PREPARE` message to each participant. Each participant checks whether it can commit: it writes the transaction's updates to its durable log (write-ahead log), takes the necessary locks, and replies `YES` (prepared) or `NO` (abort). Crucially, once a participant votes `YES`, it has promised to commit if asked — it cannot change its mind, even if it later discovers a problem. The participant must hold its locks and keep the prepared transaction in its log until it receives the coordinator's phase-2 decision. If the participant crashes after voting yes, on recovery it must re-establish the prepared state from its log and continue waiting. This is the source of the blocking problem: the participant has tied its hands by promising to commit, and it cannot unilaterally abort without risking an inconsistent outcome (the coordinator may have already decided to commit based on the yes vote).

Phase 2 is the **Commit** or **Abort** phase. The coordinator collects all votes. If all participants voted yes, the coordinator writes a `COMMIT` record to its own durable log, then sends `COMMIT` to each participant. If any participant voted no (or did not respond within a timeout), the coordinator writes an `ABORT` record and sends `ABORT` to all participants that voted yes (participants that voted no have already aborted locally). Each participant, upon receiving `COMMIT` or `ABORT`, applies the decision to its log, releases its locks, and sends an `ACK`. Once the coordinator has received all ACKs (or timed out waiting), it considers the transaction complete and writes an `end-of-transaction` record. The protocol guarantees atomicity: either all participants commit or none do, because the decision is made by the coordinator after all votes are in, and the decision is durable (logged) before being sent.

The blocking problem is the protocol's Achilles' heel. Consider a participant `P` that voted yes in phase 1, and is now waiting for the coordinator's phase-2 decision. If the coordinator crashes (or is unreachable due to a network partition) before sending the decision, `P` cannot decide on its own. It does not know whether other participants voted yes or no — if it commits unilaterally and others aborted, the transaction is inconsistent; if it aborts unilaterally and others committed, same problem. So `P` holds its locks and waits. The wait can last until the coordinator recovers, which can be minutes (coordinator restart) to hours (coordinator's storage failure requiring restore from backup). During this wait, any other transaction that needs the locked data blocks, potentially cascading into a system-wide stall. This is the "blocking on coordinator failure" problem, and it is why 2PC is rarely used in microservices: the coordinator is a single point of failure, and its failure manifests as a system-wide lock-up.

The real-world anchor is XA transactions in Java EE applications. A classic example is a transaction that updates an Oracle database and publishes a message to an IBM MQ queue: the JTA transaction manager (the coordinator) prepares both resources, and if both vote yes, commits both. The pattern works well within a single datacenter where the coordinator is highly available (often a clustered app server), but it has well-known operational pain points. PostgreSQL's `PREPARE TRANSACTION` and `COMMIT PREPARED` expose the 2PC protocol directly; `pg_prepared_xacts` is the system view that lists in-progress prepared transactions, and a lingering entry there is a classic production incident (often caused by a crashed application that did not call `COMMIT PREPARED` or `ROLLBACK PREPARED`). MySQL's `XA START`, `XA END`, `XA PREPARE`, `XA COMMIT` is the equivalent. The operational lesson is that 2PC requires monitoring of prepared transactions, runbooks for manual resolution, and a high-availability coordinator — and even with all of these, the blocking behavior on coordinator failure is a real availability risk.

The trade-off matrix for 2PC is: strong atomicity (good), strong isolation via locks (good), but blocking on coordinator failure (bad), high latency from two round-trips per transaction (bad), and operational complexity from prepared-transaction monitoring (bad). 3PC attempts to fix the blocking problem with a third phase and timeouts, but 3PC fails under network partitions (the very scenario it claims to handle), so it is rarely used in practice. Modern microservices prefer the Saga pattern, which is non-blocking but provides only eventual consistency. The architect's rule: use 2PC only when strong ACID atomicity across a small number of resources (typically 2-3) within a single datacenter is non-negotiable, the coordinator can be made highly available, and the operational burden of prepared-transaction monitoring is acceptable. For everything else, use saga or TCC. When 2PC is the right choice, invest in the operational tooling: monitor prepared transactions, alert on any entry older than a few seconds, have a runbook for manual resolution, and test coordinator failover regularly.

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Coordinator
    participant P1 as Participant 1
    participant P2 as Participant 2
    participant P3 as Participant 3

    Note over C,P3: Phase 1: PREPARE (Voting)
    C->>P1: PREPARE
    C->>P2: PREPARE
    C->>P3: PREPARE
    P1-->>C: YES (prepared, locks held)
    P2-->>C: YES (prepared, locks held)
    P3-->>C: YES (prepared, locks held)

    Note over C: Coordinator logs COMMIT decision
    Note over C,P3: Phase 2: COMMIT
    C->>P1: COMMIT
    C->>P2: COMMIT
    C->>P3: COMMIT
    P1-->>C: ACK
    P2-->>C: ACK
    P3-->>C: ACK
    Note over C: Logs end-of-transaction

    Note over C,P3: Blocking failure case (right side)
    Note over C: If coordinator crashes after phase 1
    Note over P1,P3: Participants hold locks indefinitely
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
   Phase 1: PREPARE               Phase 2: COMMIT
   +-----------+                  +-----------+
   |Coord      |                  |Coord      |
   +-----+-----+                  +-----+-----+
         |                              |
   PREPARE|PREPARE  PREPARE       COMMIT|COMMIT COMMIT
         v       v   v                 v       v   v
     +---+---+ +---+---+ +---+---+ +---+---+ +---+---+ +---+---+
     | P1:YES| | P2:YES| | P3:NO | | P1:COM| | P2:COM| | P3:ABT|
     +---+---+ +---+---+ +---+---+ +---+---+ +---+---+ +---+---+
         ^                                |
         |   (locks held until phase 2)   |
         +--------------------------------+

   BLOCKING failure: coordinator crashes between phase 1 and phase 2
   +-----------+
   |Coord DOWN |   (no COMMIT, no ABORT sent)
   +-----------+
       P1: YES  (holds locks, waits...)   <- blocked
       P2: YES  (holds locks, waits...)   <- blocked
       P3: YES  (holds locks, waits...)   <- blocked
```

### Walkthrough
1. The coordinator sends `PREPARE` to all three participants in phase 1. Each participant writes its updates to its durable log, takes locks, and replies `YES` (or `NO` if it cannot commit). Once a participant votes `YES`, it is bound to that vote and must hold its locks.
2. The coordinator collects the votes. If all are `YES`, it writes a `COMMIT` decision to its own durable log and sends `COMMIT` to each participant in phase 2. If any vote was `NO` or timed out, it writes `ABORT` and sends `ABORT` instead.
3. Each participant applies the decision, releases its locks, and sends `ACK`. If the coordinator crashes after phase 1 but before phase 2, participants that voted `YES` are blocked — they hold their locks indefinitely, waiting for the coordinator to recover and send the decision. This is the blocking failure mode that makes 2PC unsuitable for high-availability microservices.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
Two Phase Commit (2PC) coordinator + participant state machine.
Demonstrates the prepare/commit/abort flow and the blocking failure case.
"""
import enum

class State(enum.Enum):
    INITIAL = "INITIAL"
    PREPARED = "PREPARED"     # voted YES, holding locks
    COMMITTED = "COMMITTED"
    ABORTED = "ABORTED"

class Participant:
    """A 2PC participant with a local durable log."""
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.state = State.INITIAL
        self.will_prepare = True     # configurable for the demo

    def prepare(self):
        if not self.will_prepare:
            self.state = State.ABORTED
            print(f"  [{self.name}] PREPARE -> NO (aborting locally)")
            return False
        # Write to durable log, take locks.
        self.state = State.PREPARED
        print(f"  [{self.name}] PREPARE -> YES (locks held, log written)")
        return True

    def commit(self):
        assert self.state == State.PREPARED
        self.state = State.COMMITTED
        print(f"  [{self.name}] COMMIT -> applied, locks released")
        return True

    def abort(self):
        self.state = State.ABORTED
        print(f"  [{self.name}] ABORT -> rolled back, locks released")
        return True

class Coordinator:
    """2PC coordinator with a durable decision log."""
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.decision_log = []        # durable: survives crashes
        self.alive = True

    def execute(self, txid, participants):
        if not self.alive:
            print(f"[{self.name}] coordinator DOWN -> blocked")
            return "BLOCKED"
        print(f"[{self.name}] phase 1: PREPARE txid={txid}")
        votes = [p.prepare() for p in participants]
        if all(votes):
            self.decision_log.append(("COMMIT", txid))   # durable decision
            print(f"[{self.name}] phase 2: COMMIT txid={txid}")
            for p in participants:
                p.commit()
            return "COMMITTED"
        else:
            self.decision_log.append(("ABORT", txid))
            print(f"[{self.name}] phase 2: ABORT txid={txid}")
            for p in participants:
                if p.state == State.PREPARED:
                    p.abort()
            return "ABORTED"

# --- Demo: successful commit ---
print("=== Successful 2PC ===")
c = Coordinator("C1")
ps = [Participant("P1"), Participant("P2"), Participant("P3")]
c.execute("TX1", ps)

# --- Demo: abort due to a NO vote ---
print("\n=== 2PC with abort ===")
c2 = Coordinator("C2")
ps2 = [Participant("P1"), Participant("P2"), Participant("P3")]
ps2[1].will_prepare = False           # P2 votes NO
c2.execute("TX2", ps2)

# --- Demo: blocking failure (coordinator crashes after prepare) ---
print("\n=== 2PC blocking failure ===")
c3 = Coordinator("C3")
ps3 = [Participant("P1"), Participant("P2"), Participant("P3")]
print("[C3] phase 1: PREPARE txid=TX3")
for p in ps3:
    p.prepare()                        # all participants prepared, locks held
c3.alive = False                       # coordinator crashes before phase 2
c3.execute("TX3", ps3)                 # participants blocked, holding locks
print("  (P1, P2, P3 hold locks indefinitely until C3 recovers)")
```
